title: Global Macro
summary: Discretionary bets on rates, currencies and policy — few positions, large sizes, and convictions that can be right too early.

lesson.body:
[[global-macro]] managers take views on the big variables — interest rates, currencies, sovereign credit, commodities, equity indices — and express them wherever the trade is cleanest. A view on tightening policy might be expressed in rate futures, in a currency, in a [[yield-curve]] steepener, or in equity index options, chosen on liquidity and payoff shape rather than on which asset class the manager nominally belongs to.

Two features follow from this and define the strategy.

**Breadth of instruments, narrowness of positions.** A macro fund can trade almost anything, and typically holds few large positions rather than many small ones. Concentration is the point: these are conviction views, not a diversified harvest.

**Derivatives-heavy, capital-light.** Rate futures, FX forwards and options give large notional exposure for modest margin. So the fund's [[net-asset-value]] tells you very little about the size of its bets, and headline exposure figures need care.

**The return driver is being right about a macro variable before the market reprices it.** Not carry, not a risk premium harvested mechanically — a directional judgement about policy, growth, inflation or capital flows.

That makes the strategy fundamentally different from most of the arbitrage strategies. There is no convergence mechanism, no deal to close, no spread that mathematically must narrow. If the manager is wrong, nothing brings the position back.

It also makes returns lumpy. A macro fund can spend eighteen months making very little while positioned for a regime change that has not arrived, then produce most of a multi-year return in a single quarter when it does. Judging such a manager on a two-year window is close to meaningless, which is an uncomfortable fact given how allocation decisions are usually made.

The characteristic macro failure is not being wrong. It is being **right too early**, which is operationally indistinguishable from being wrong.

A manager identifies that a currency peg is unsustainable, or that inflation will force a policy reversal, and positions accordingly. The thesis is correct. But the repricing takes two years longer than expected, and in the meantime the position bleeds — through [[carry]], through option decay, through margin calls as it moves against them. The fund is down, investors redeem, and the manager reduces or exits. Then the thesis plays out for someone else.

This is why **position sizing and staying power matter more than analysis** in this strategy. Two managers with identical, correct theses can produce opposite outcomes purely on how much they risked and whether their capital base survived the wait. When you assess a macro manager, you are assessing three things: the quality of the view, the discipline of the sizing, and the stability of the capital behind it.

lesson.caption: What helps and what hurts
rows: Creates large, tradeable dislocations in rates and currencies — the strategy's core raw material.
Forces policy responses, which is exactly what macro managers position for.
More carry to earn or pay, and more variation across countries to trade against each other.
Nothing to trade. Long periods of stable, well-telegraphed policy starve the strategy of opportunity.
Central bank intervention against a thesis
An authority with an unlimited balance sheet can defer a repricing far longer than a fund can fund the position.
Macro books often share crowded positioning, and levered positions get reduced together.

lesson.body:
**Leverage against a slow thesis.** The classic path. Notional exposure through derivatives is cheap to acquire, so a manager can hold a position far larger than their capital would suggest. If the repricing is delayed, financing costs and margin calls force reduction before the thesis pays.

**Concentration.** Few positions means one wrong call can dominate. Macro drawdowns of 20% or more from a single theme are not unusual, and the strategy's structure makes them hard to avoid entirely.

**Fighting a central bank.** A policy authority defending a peg or a rate can sustain a position indefinitely in a way a leveraged fund cannot. Being economically correct and financially destroyed at the same time is a real outcome.

**Liquidity mismatch in the tail.** Macro managers often trade some less liquid expressions — emerging market local rates, off-the-run instruments, certain options — for better payoff. Those are precisely the markets that gap in stress, so the exit is worst when it is most needed.

**Redemption pressure at the worst point.** Because returns are lumpy, investors tend to redeem after quiet or losing periods, which is often just before the thesis pays. The manager is then forced to cut the position that was about to work.

**Do not read a macro fund's exposure the way you read an equity fund's.** A 300% notional figure in rate futures is not comparable to 300% gross in equities — the volatility per unit of notional is completely different. A two-year interest rate future moves a fraction of what an equity position does.

The meaningful measures are risk-based rather than notional: contribution to volatility by theme, or [[value-at-risk]] by risk factor. When a macro manager quotes notional exposure without translating it into risk, that is worth pressing on, and the translation is a reasonable thing to ask them to provide.

**Ask what the manager's largest theme is and what it would cost if the timing is wrong by a year.** That single answer tells you more about the fund than any risk report.

**Judge the process over the horizon it operates on.** A three-year assessment window for a manager whose theses take three to five years to play out will systematically fire the ones about to be right. If you cannot commit for the horizon, this may not be the right strategy rather than the right manager being unavailable.

**Understand the investor base.** A macro fund whose capital is redemption-prone is materially weaker than one with locked or patient capital, holding the identical portfolio. Staying power is part of the investment case here in a way it is not for a liquid arbitrage strategy.

**Look for evidence of sizing discipline in past losses.** A manager who cut a losing thesis at a defined level, and can explain the rule, is demonstrating the thing that actually determines survival. One who describes adding all the way down is telling you about the drawdown you will eventually experience.

items: The return driver is a correct directional judgement about a macro variable. There is no convergence mechanism to rescue a wrong position.
Being right too early is the characteristic failure and is indistinguishable from being wrong while it is happening.
Notional exposure is not comparable to equity gross exposure. Insist on risk-based measures by theme.
Sizing discipline and stable capital matter as much as the quality of the view, because both determine whether the fund survives the wait.

questions.stem: What most distinguishes global macro from an arbitrage strategy like merger arbitrage?
choices: Macro positions rely on a directional judgement with no mechanism forcing convergence
Macro funds do not use leverage
Macro funds hold many more positions
Macro returns are more predictable quarter to quarter
rationales: Correct. A merger spread narrows because a deal closes; a macro view pays only if the market comes round to it. Nothing mathematically compels that, which changes the whole risk character.
Macro funds are typically heavy users of derivatives leverage — notional exposure is often a large multiple of capital.
The reverse. Macro books are usually concentrated in a handful of high-conviction themes, while merger arb books hold dozens of deals.
Macro returns are notably lumpy: long quiet stretches then large moves. Predictability is not a feature.
questions.explanation: The absence of a convergence mechanism is the defining feature. It means a macro position can stay wrong indefinitely, which is why sizing and staying power dominate the risk conversation.

questions.stem: "A macro manager whose thesis eventually proved correct was a good manager, even if the fund lost money waiting." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — being right too early is operationally the same as being wrong if the position could not be held to the payoff
False — a thesis that takes years to play out was not a real thesis
True — the analysis was correct, and that is what defines skill
False — because macro theses can never be verified after the fact
rationales: Correct. Analysis is only half the job. If the position was sized so that financing costs and margin calls forced an exit before the repricing, the investor lost money on a correct view — and the sizing was the error.
Long-horizon theses are entirely legitimate in macro. The issue is matching position size and capital stability to that horizon.
This is the misconception. Skill in this strategy is the analysis *plus* the sizing plus surviving the wait. A view you cannot hold is not an investable view.
Theses often can be verified afterwards — the currency did devalue, the policy did reverse. That is what makes the too-early failure so galling.
questions.explanation: This is the sharpest lesson in the strategy. Two managers with identical correct theses can produce opposite results purely through position sizing and capital stability, which is why diligence focuses on both rather than on the quality of the argument alone.

questions.stem: A macro fund reports 320% notional exposure. Why is comparing that with an equity fund's 320% gross exposure misleading?
choices: Notional figures are always overstated by derivative accounting
Volatility per unit of notional differs enormously — a short-dated rate future moves a fraction of what an equity position does
Macro funds mark their positions less frequently
Equity gross exposure excludes shorts while notional exposure includes them
rationales: Notional is a factual measure of contract size, not an accounting distortion. The problem is what it implies about risk, not its accuracy.

Correct. $100 of two-year rate future exposure carries a small fraction of the risk of $100 of equity. Equal notional figures can mean wildly different risk, which is why risk-based measures are the meaningful ones here.
Macro instruments are typically exchange-traded and liquid, so marking frequency is not the issue.
Gross exposure includes shorts by definition. That is not the distinction.
questions.explanation: Notional exposure answers "how much contract have I got?" rather than "how much can I lose?". For a fund trading instruments with radically different volatilities, only risk-based measures — contribution to volatility, or VaR by factor — support comparison.

questions.description: A fund returned roughly 1% a year for three consecutive years with low volatility, then +34% in a single year during a period of rapid policy tightening. It holds fewer than ten meaningful positions, mostly in interest rate futures and currency forwards, with notional exposure several times capital and margin usage under 20%.
choices: Discretionary global macro
Fixed income relative value
Equity market neutral
Merger arbitrage
rationales: Correct. Every marker fits: very few positions, rates and FX instruments, notional far exceeding capital on light margin, years of little happening followed by an outsized year when the regime turned.
Fixed income relative value trades spreads between related instruments for convergence, producing steadier returns and far more positions than ten — and it does not typically post a +34% year.
Market neutral holds hundreds of equity positions and targets steady low-volatility returns. Nothing here matches.
Merger arb holds dozens of deals and has a bounded upside per position. A +34% year is not achievable from spread capture.
questions.explanation: The lumpy return pattern is the strongest single clue. Three flat years and one enormous one is the signature of directional conviction waiting for a regime change — and the reason judging these managers over short windows is close to useless.

questions.stem: A macro fund is short a currency it judges to be overvalued and defended at an unsustainable level. Why is this position dangerous even if the analysis is right?
choices: Currency positions cannot be sized accurately
A central bank can defend the level far longer than a leveraged fund can fund the position
Short currency positions have unlimited upside
Central banks always win currency defences
rationales: Currency positions can be sized precisely. Sizing is a discipline issue, not a measurement one.

Correct. The asymmetry is about balance sheets and time. An authority with the capacity to intervene can defer a repricing for years, while the fund pays carry and meets margin calls throughout. Economically correct and financially finished is a real outcome.
This confuses a short currency position with a short equity position. A currency cannot rise without limit, and that is not the mechanism at work.
Not true — defences do fail, sometimes spectacularly. The danger is the timing, not the eventual outcome.
questions.explanation: This is the macro version of the market's oldest lesson: solvency has to outlast being right. A thesis you cannot fund to its conclusion is a thesis you cannot invest in, however good the analysis.

questions.stem: Two macro managers hold identical portfolios. One has locked capital with three-year commitments; the other offers monthly liquidity to a redemption-prone investor base. What follows?
choices: Nothing — the portfolios are identical, so the return outcomes should match
The manager with patient capital is materially more likely to realise the theses, because they will not be forced to cut during a drawdown
The monthly-liquidity manager is better, because liquidity is always valuable to investors
The difference only matters if the portfolios contain illiquid instruments
rationales: Identical portfolios do not imply identical outcomes when one manager may be forced to sell mid-thesis. The capital base is part of the strategy, not a wrapper around it.

Correct. Because macro returns are lumpy, redemptions cluster after quiet or losing stretches — often just before the thesis pays. Being forced to reduce then converts a correct view into a realised loss.
Liquidity is valuable to an investor considered alone, but offering it against a long-horizon strategy creates exactly the forced-selling risk that destroys the returns being sought.
It matters even with fully liquid instruments. The problem is being made to exit at the wrong time, not being unable to exit.
questions.explanation: Terms are part of the investment case in this strategy. A liquidity profile mismatched to the horizon of the theses is a structural weakness that no amount of analytical skill compensates for.
